(CNN) -- Jenny's phone number is for sale, but not for a song. "867-5309/Jenny" originally appeared on Tommy Tutone's "Tommy Tutone 2" album. Bids for a New Jersey version of the number, stuck in the minds of millions since Tommy Tutone's "867-5309/Jenny" hit the Top 10 in 1982, had reached $5,100 on eBay as of Monday morning. The song is about a guy who finds Jenny's name and number scribbled on a bathroom wall. "This is really, in my opinion, one of the last cultural remnants of the '80s pop culture era ... other than the mullet," said Spencer Potter, a 28-year-old DJ who is selling the number he got for free five years ago. While Potter is overlooking the fact that "867-5309" is an active phone number in dozens of other area codes, it does get called a lot by curious people. Potter said he has gotten about 40 calls a day since he got the area code 201 version for his Weehawken, New Jersey, DJ business. "The minute we plugged the phone jack into the wall, it began ringing," Potter said. Mostly, Potter said, the callers are "a lot of '80s fanatics" and he lets the calls ring through to his voice mail. When he did answer a call three years ago, Potter found his own Jenny on the line. "She had been using my number to give out to guys that she didn't like at bars," he said. "It was a bum phone number." The young lady from Hoboken, New Jersey, told Potter she was just curious about who might be getting the calls. Potter ended up asking her out. "I figured if she was having to give out a bum number that often then she was probably pretty cute," he said. "We ended up meeting for drinks. We dated for awhile and it was actually a great friendship." Potter recently moved from Weehawken and decided to try to make money off the infamous digits with an eBay auction. Potter's DJ business goes with the number, a necessary provision to get around phone company rules against selling telephone numbers, he said. Phone companies technically own the numbers, not the customers. Potter said Vonage, the company that assigned the number, gave him permission to transfer it as part of the sale of his business. EBay halted a 2004 auction by the purported holder of the 212 area code version of the number, The New York Times reported. A Philadelphia-area resident who holds the toll-free versions -- both 800 and 888 -- said he values his numbers in the millions. Jeffrey Steinberg said his best offer so far, rejected several years ago, was for $1 million from a national weight-loss company. He acquired the numbers in the early 1990s for a pizza delivery campaign and has licensed them for other advertisers in the years since. Potter said when his auction ends next Monday, February 9, he hopes to make at least $40,000. He said he would use the money to take a Caribbean vacation -- away from his ringing phone. . CNN's Laurie Segall and CNN Radio's April Williams contributed to this report.

# The Legendary Jenny Number Hits the Auction Block

(CNN) -- Jenny's phone number is up for sale—though not, as the song might suggest, for a mere song. "867-5309/Jenny" first graced the airwaves on Tommy Tutone's album "Tommy Tutone 2," and the tune has since embedded itself in the collective memory of millions since climbing into the Top 10 in 1982. Now, a New Jersey version of that iconic number has attracted bids reaching $5,100 on eBay as of Monday morning.

The song tells the story of a man who discovers Jenny's name and number scrawled on a bathroom wall. "This is really, in my opinion, one of the last cultural remnants of the '80s pop culture era... other than the mullet," remarked Spencer Potter, the 28-year-old DJ selling the number he acquired free of charge five years ago.

Though Potter overlooks the fact that "867-5309" remains an active number across dozens of other area codes, his particular version certainly attracts its share of curious callers. Potter reports receiving roughly 40 calls daily since obtaining the area code 201 version for his DJ business in Weehawken, New Jersey. "The minute we plugged the phone jack into the wall, it began ringing," he recalled.

According to Potter, most callers are simply "'80s fanatics," and he typically allows these calls to roll over to voicemail. However, when he answered one such call three years ago, he found himself speaking with his very own Jenny. "She had been using my number to give out to guys that she didn't like at bars," he explained. "It was a bum phone number."

The young woman, a Hoboken, New Jersey resident, told Potter she was merely curious about who might be receiving these misdirected calls. Potter, intrigued, ultimately asked her out. "I figured if she was having to give out a bum number that often, she was probably pretty cute," he said. "We ended up meeting for drinks. We dated for a while, and it actually blossomed into a great friendship."

Having recently relocated from Weehawken, Potter decided to capitalize on the number's notoriety by launching an eBay auction. Notably, his DJ business is included in the sale—a necessary arrangement to comply with phone company regulations prohibiting the direct sale of telephone numbers, since carriers technically retain ownership of the numbers themselves, not the customers who use them. Potter noted that Vonage, the company that originally assigned him the number, granted permission for its transfer as part of the business sale.

This isn't the first time such a sale has generated controversy: eBay halted a similar 2004 auction by the purported holder of the number's 212 area code version, according to The New York Times.

Meanwhile, a Philadelphia-area resident who holds both the 800 and 888 toll-free versions of the number values his numbers in the millions. Jeffrey Steinberg revealed that his best offer to date—rejected several years ago—came from a national weight-loss company willing to pay $1 million. Steinberg originally acquired the numbers in the early 1990s for a pizza delivery campaign and has since licensed them to various other advertisers.

As for Potter, when his auction concludes next Monday, February 9, he's hoping to net at least $40,000—proceeds he plans to put toward a Caribbean vacation, far away from his perpetually ringing phone.

*CNN's Laurie Segall and CNN Radio's April Williams contributed to this report.*

# Jenny, Tommy, and the CNN Mystery

Jenny and Tommy were neighbors who shared a passion for technology and had recently started learning about artificial intelligence together. Every Saturday afternoon, they would meet at the local library to work on their latest project: understanding how computers could "see" and recognize images.

It was Tommy who first stumbled upon the concept of CNNs—Convolutional Neural Networks—while researching for their school science fair project. He excitedly showed Jenny an article explaining how these networks could identify cats, dogs, and even handwritten numbers just by analyzing patterns in pixels.

"Look at this, Jenny!" Tommy said, pointing at his laptop screen. "A CNN works kind of like how our eyes and brain work together. It scans small parts of an image first, then combines that information to understand the whole picture!"

Jenny, who loved drawing diagrams to understand complex ideas, immediately began sketching out how the layers of a CNN might work. She drew boxes representing convolutional layers, pooling layers, and finally the fully connected layer that would make the final decision about what the image showed.

Together, they decided to build a simple CNN model using Python for their science fair project. Tommy focused on writing the code, while Jenny researched datasets they could use to train their network. They chose a collection of images featuring different types of flowers, hoping their CNN could learn to distinguish between roses, daisies, and tulips.

The project wasn't without challenges. Their first few attempts resulted in the CNN confusing tulips with roses, and Tommy grew frustrated when the accuracy rate stayed below fifty percent. Jenny suggested they add more layers to the network and adjust the learning rate, remembering something she'd read about how these adjustments could help the model learn more effectively.

After several weeks of tweaking parameters and running training sessions late into the evening, their persistence paid off. The CNN's accuracy climbed to an impressive ninety-two percent. Jenny and Tommy were thrilled when they tested it on new flower images the network had never seen before, and it correctly identified almost all of them.

At the science fair, their project stood out among classmates who had chosen more traditional topics. Judges were impressed not only by the technical achievement but also by how clearly Jenny and Tommy could explain the underlying concepts of convolutional neural networks—how the network learned to recognize edges, then shapes, and finally complex patterns unique to each flower type.

Their teacher, impressed by their dedication, encouraged them to continue exploring machine learning topics. Jenny and Tommy left the science fair with a first-place ribbon, but more importantly, they had discovered something valuable: the exciting world of artificial intelligence, and how understanding it could open doors to solving countless real-world problems.

That night, as they celebrated their win with ice cream, Tommy turned to Jenny and said, "This is just the beginning. Imagine what we could build next!" Jenny smiled, already sketching ideas for their next project in her notebook—perhaps this time, teaching a CNN to recognize different types of birds in their backyard.

# Iconic "867-5309" Phone Number Hits eBay, Bidders Dial Up Nostalgia

**By CNN Staff**

A phone number immortalized in one of the most recognizable songs of the 1980s is now up for grabs — for a price.

The digits 867-5309, made famous by Tommy Tutone's 1982 hit "867-5309/Jenny," have appeared in an eBay listing that has quickly gone viral, drawing thousands of views and a flurry of bids from music fans, collectors, and pranksters alike.

The seller, who claims to hold the rights to a mobile number matching the iconic sequence in a specific area code, describes the listing as a "once-in-a-lifetime piece of pop culture history." The auction description reads: "Own the number millions have shouted, sung, and prank-called for over 40 years. Perfect for businesses, collectors, or anyone who wants their phone to ring off the hook — literally."

"867-5309/Jenny" reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and has remained a karaoke and classic rock radio staple ever since. The song's infectious hook turned the number into an instant novelty, prompting decades of prank calls to anyone unfortunate enough to be assigned it. Numerous businesses and individuals across the country have reported being flooded with calls over the years simply because their number contained the famous digits.

Telecom experts note that phone numbers themselves generally can't be legally "sold" outright in the traditional sense, since carriers technically own and assign numbers to customers. However, sellers can offer to facilitate a transfer process — often called "porting" — to a buyer for a fee, which appears to be the arrangement being proposed in this listing.

As of Tuesday afternoon, bidding had surpassed $1,500, with eBay users leaving comments ranging from enthusiastic ("Finally, I can BE Jenny") to skeptical, with some questioning whether the transfer would actually be honored by carriers.

Tommy Tutone, the band behind the original hit, has not commented on the sale.

The auction is set to close later this week. Whether the winning bidder will actually get a working line remains to be seen — but for now, the listing has succeeded in doing what the song has done for over four decades: getting stuck in everyone's head.

*CNN has reached out to eBay for comment on the listing and its compliance with the platform's policies regarding the sale of telecommunications services.*

# The Digits That Launched a Thousand Prank Calls: DJ Auctions Off "867-5309"

## Iconic Phone Number Immortalized by Tommy Tutone Hits the Market

For over four decades, anyone unlucky enough to be assigned the phone number 867-5309 has fielded a peculiar kind of harassment: strangers calling just to see if "Jenny" would pick up. Now, a radio DJ who has held the coveted digits for years is putting them up for sale, hoping to cash in on one of pop music's most enduring novelty hits.

Mark Rutherford, a longtime radio personality who goes by "DJ Rudy" on-air, acquired the number for his cell phone nearly fifteen years ago as a gag—and it's been ringing off the hook ever since.

"I got it as kind of a joke from a buddy who worked at the phone company," Rutherford said. "I figured I'd get a few calls a week, maybe some laughs at parties. I did not anticipate strangers calling me at 2 a.m. from three time zones away asking for Jenny."

## The Song That Started It All

Released in 1981, "867-5309/Jenny" by Tommy Tutone became an unlikely chart-topping hit, reaching No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100. The song, written by band members Alex Call and Jim Keller, tells the story of a man who finds a phone number scrawled on a bathroom wall—"Jenny, Jenny, who can I turn to?"—and becomes infatuated with the mysterious woman attached to it.

The song's infectious hook and singable chorus turned the fictional phone number into real-world catnip. Across the country, people with that combination of digits—regardless of area code—have spent decades fielding calls from pranksters, curious fans, and drunk partygoers convinced they might actually reach Jenny.

"It's one of those songs that everybody knows, even people who weren't born when it came out," said music historian Diane Castellano. "The number became bigger than the song itself in a lot of ways. It's rare for a piece of pop culture to have a literal, tangible artifact like that—something people can actually call."

## Cashing In on Novelty

Rutherford says the constant calls—sometimes dozens a day, especially around the song's anniversary or when it pops up in a movie or commercial—finally became more trouble than they were worth.

"I love the attention, don't get me wrong. I've made friends this way. I once got invited to a wedding because the groom was obsessed with the song," he laughed. "But my phone was basically unusable as an actual phone. I'd miss calls from my mom because some guy from Ohio wanted to sing me the chorus."

Rutherford has listed the number for sale, marketing it to collectors, marketers, and even other radio stations that might want to use it for promotions or contests. He's fielding offers starting in the low five figures, though he declined to specify an asking price.

"There's a real market for numbers like this," said telecom broker Sandra Weiss, who specializes in vanity and novelty numbers. "Anything with cultural cachet—especially something tied to music, sports, or a famous event—can command serious money. This one's about as recognizable as it gets."

## A Bittersweet Goodbye

Despite the headaches, Rutherford admits he's a little sentimental about giving up the number.

"It's a piece of Americana, honestly," he said. "Every time that phone rings and someone starts singing to me, it's this weird little moment of connection with a total stranger. We're both in on the same joke."

Still, he's ready to pass the torch—and the ringtone.

"Whoever buys it better have a good voicemail message ready," Rutherford said. "Because trust me, they're going to need it."

---

*Tommy Tutone's "867-5309/Jenny" remains a staple of classic rock radio and '80s nostalgia playlists, proving that sometimes the most powerful lyrics in pop music are just a string of numbers.*

**The digits "867-5309" have never really belonged to anyone — until now**

For 40 years, anyone unlucky enough to be assigned the phone number ending in 867-5309 has lived a peculiar kind of purgatory: constant prank calls, confused texts asking for "Jenny," and the occasional stranger just singing the chorus of a one-hit wonder into their voicemail.

An eBay auction for a phone number containing the sequence 867-5309 — immortalized by Tommy Tutone's 1981 new wave hit "867-5309/Jenny" — recently closed at a price that underscores just how much nostalgia, novelty, and pop culture cachet can be worth in the world of vanity phone numbers.

## The Song That Wouldn't Die

"867-5309/Jenny" spent weeks on the Billboard charts in 1982, propelled by its irresistibly catchy hook and a phone number that listeners couldn't stop dialing — even though it wasn't real, or so songwriters Alex Call and Jim Keller thought. In the decades since, the combination has become one of the most recognizable strings of digits in American pop culture, right up there with 555-2368 (the Ghostbusters hotline, also fictional).

The real-world consequences for anyone actually issued that number have been well-documented. Restaurants, businesses, and private citizens who received phone lines ending in 867-5309 have reported being bombarded with calls from pranksters and curious fans for years — sometimes forcing them to change their numbers entirely just for peace of mind.

So when a number containing that exact sequence popped up for sale, bidders apparently saw opportunity rather than nuisance — perhaps eyeing it for marketing purposes, novelty value, or simple collector's pride.

## Not the First Numeric Novelty to Cash In

This isn't the first time a phone number has fetched a premium price. Vanity and "trophy" numbers have become their own peculiar corner of the collectibles market, particularly in regions like Hong Kong, mainland China, and the Middle East, where numerology and superstition often drive up prices to eye-watering levels.

In Hong Kong, telecom carriers have auctioned off numbers featuring repeating lucky digits — particularly those containing multiple 8s, considered auspicious in Chinese culture because the word for "eight" sounds similar to the word for "prosperity." Some of these numbers have sold for hundreds of thousands of dollars. In 2016, a Hong Kong businessman reportedly paid **$280,000** for a single mobile number consisting entirely of the digit 9, repeated multiple times.

Qatar has also seen numbers fetch huge sums: in 2006, the number "666-6666" sold at a charity auction for a staggering **$2.75 million**, setting a record at the time for the most expensive phone number ever sold.

In the U.S., vanity numbers tend to trade for far more modest sums, typically ranging from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars, and are usually driven by business branding value (think 1-800-FLOWERS) rather than pop culture nostalgia.

## Why Jenny's Number Is Different

What makes the 867-5309 sale unique is that its value isn't rooted in luck, numerology, or memorability for commercial branding — it's rooted entirely in a 40-year-old song that has embedded itself so deeply into American consciousness that the mere sequence of numbers triggers a Pavlovian singalong.

It joins a strange lineage of numbers that have transcended their function as mere contact information to become cultural artifacts in their own right — evidence that in the digital age, even a string of digits can become a monument to nostalgia, kitsch, and collective memory.

Whoever now owns the "Jenny" number should probably brace themselves. Somewhere, a Tommy Tutone fan is bound to call — just to see if she'll pick up.
